title: The recommended threshold table assigns the lowest signing threshold to the highest-impact use case
content:
A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.4 tabulates recommended thresholds against both classification axes: Treasury-Large (High / Routine) 4/7; Treasury-Small (Medium / Routine) 3/5; Emergency Freeze (Critical / Emergency) 2/4; Capital Allocation (High / Time-Sensitive) 3/5; Protocol Parameters (High / Routine) 4/7; Constrained DeFi (Medium / Time-Sensitive) 2/3.

Read down the Impact column alone, the table looks backwards. The only use case graded Critical carries the second-lowest threshold in the set, and Constrained DeFi at merely Medium impact sits at 2/3. Any framework that mapped criticality monotonically onto threshold would produce the opposite ordering.

The pattern resolves once the Operational axis is read as the dominant term. Every Routine case gets a majority-of-seven or majority-of-five; every Time-Sensitive or Emergency case is relaxed to a bare two-signer requirement. Impact grades the *consequence* of failure, but the threshold is set by the *time available* to assemble signatures — and a <2 hour response window cannot wait for five of seven people.

The compensating controls are what make this defensible rather than reckless: Emergency Freeze multisigs cannot move assets (A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.2.3.2), and Constrained DeFi is bounded on-chain. So the table only appears to invert risk. It is really applying the substitution principle — where capability is limited, threshold can be too.

These are labelled recommendations that "serve as guidance to the Multisig Administrator," not requirements, which means the self-assessed classification chosen under A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.1.1 selects the row and therefore the threshold.
description: Emergency Freeze is graded Critical impact yet recommended at 2/4, while Treasury-Large at High impact gets 4/7 — because the Operational axis, not the Impact axis, drives the threshold.
